claim: TRBP2-dsRBD1 and TRBP2-dsRBD2 share 30% identity and 38% similarity in their primary sequences.
source: Primary sequence comparison of TRBP2-dsRBD1 and TRBP2-dsRBD2 domain constructs (Figure 1A) revealed 30% identity and 38% similarity.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on sequence comparison analysis performed by the authors.

claim: The two reported RNA-binding regions 1 (E) and 3 (KKxAK) of both dsRBD1 and dsRBD2 match the consensus sequence.
source: The two reported RNA-binding regions 1 (E) and 3 (KKxAK) of both the domains were matched to the consensus (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B showing sequence alignment.

claim: TRBP2-dsRBD1 harbors a mutation in RNA-binding region 2 (P56Q).
source: While RNA-binding region 2 (GPxH) (Figure 1B, region 2) of TRBP2-dsRBD2 was an exact match to the consensus, dsRBD1 harbored a mutation in region 2 (P56Q).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 1B.

claim: The presence of conserved Pro186 in the β1–β2 loop of dsRBD2 may perturb the β1–β2 loop region plasticity, making it more accessible to the incoming RNA partner.
source: Thus, the presence of conserved Pro186 in the β1–β2 loop of dsRBD2 (Figure 1B, region 2) may perturb the β1–β2 loop region plasticity, thereby making it more accessible to the incoming RNA partner.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on inference from the known properties of proline and the sequence data.

claim: dsRBD2 contains a KR-helix motif in the α2-helix known to increase its binding affinity.
source: Additionally, dsRBD2 contains a KR-helix motif in the α2-helix (Figure 1B, region 3) known to increase its binding affinity, as reported earlier by Daviet et al., 2000.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TRBP2-dsRBD2 exists as a single monomeric species in solution under experimental conditions.
source: The size-exclusion chromatography coupled with multiple angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) study of TRBP2-dsRBD2 in the experimental conditions used showed a single monomeric species in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by SEC-MALS experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 1H-15N HSQC spectrum of TRBP2-dsRBD2 indicated a well-folded protein.
source: The 1H-15N HSQC spectrum (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) of TRBP2-dsRBD2 indicated a well-folded protein.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A total of 73 non-proline residues were assigned in TRBP2-dsRBD2.
source: Resonance assignments were further confirmed using a set of double and triple resonance experiments, and a total of 73 non-proline residues were assigned, as shown in the representative 1H-15N HSQC (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by NMR assignment data.

claim: Overall, 89% 1H (151/169), 74% 13C (124/168), and 87% 15N (73/84) resonances from the backbone, and 43% 1H (174/402) and 25% 13C (59/238) from the side chains were assigned in TRBP2-dsRBD2.
source: Overall, 89% 1H (151/169), 74% 13C (124/168), and 87% 15N (73/84) resonances from the backbone, and 43% 1H (174/402) and 25% 13C (59/238) from the side chains were assigned.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents NMR assignment statistics.

claim: The CS-Rosetta structure of dsRBD2 matched well with previously reported structures in terms of characteristic dsRBD fold.
source: Similar to the CS-Rosetta structure calculated previously for dsRBD1 (Figure 1C) by our group (Paithankar et al., 2018), the CS-Rosetta structure calculated for the dsRBD2 (Figure 1D) matched well with the previously reported structures in terms of characteristic dsRBD fold.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The core residues (159–227 aa) of dsRBD2 adapt the characteristic dsRBD αβββα fold with an RMSD of 1.284 Å when compared to the previously reported solution structure of dsRBD2 (2CPN; Yamashita et al., 2011).
source: The core residues (159–227 aa) of dsRBD2 were found to adapt the characteristic dsRBD αβββα fold with an RMSD (root mean square deviation) of 1.284 Å when compared to the previously reported solution structure of dsRBD2 (2CPN; Yamashita et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by structural comparison data and citation.

claim: An alignment of core structures between dsRBD1 and dsRBD2 yielded an RMSD of 0.894 Å, indicating a close match between the two domains.
source: An alignment of core structures between dsRBD1 and dsRBD2 (Figure 1E) yielded an RMSD of 0.894 Å, indicating a close match between the two domains.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by structural alignment data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Loop 2 (β1–β2 loop) is equal to the canonical length in dsRBD2, while in dsRBD1, it is shorter by 1 residue.
source: Most importantly, loop 2 (β1–β2 loop) – critical for RNA binding (Masliah et al., 2013) – is equal to the canonical length in dsRBD2, while in dsRBD1, it is shorter by 1 residue (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by structural data and citation.

claim: The average RMSF of the core domain of dsRBD2 is 0.22 nm, which is almost half as compared to dsRBD1 RMSF average of 0.43.
source: Comparing the molecular dynamics (MD) simulation data of the core residue-specific RMSF (root mean square fluctuation) plots of these two type-A dsRBD domains (Figure 2A), we observe that the average RMSF of the core domain of dsRBD2 is 0.22 nm, which is almost half as compared to dsRBD1 RMSF average of 0.43.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: dsRBD2 is overall more rigid than dsRBD1 based on RMSF data.
source: This, in turn, indicates that dsRBD2 is overall more rigid among the two.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on inference from RMSF data.

claim: Loop 2 of dsRBD2 is very flexible compared to the rest of the core, with an average RMSF of 0.49 nm (more than double the core average).
source: The most interesting fact is that loop 2 (shown in Figure 1B) of dsRBD2 is very flexible compared to the rest of the core, with an average RMSF of 0.49 nm (more than double the core average), as depicted in Figure 2A.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The long, conserved, and dynamic loop 2 might help dsRBD2 to establish strong contacts in the minor grooves of dsRNA partners.
source: Hence, we propose that this long, conserved, and dynamic loop 2 might help dsRBD2 to establish strong contacts in the minor grooves of dsRNA partners.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on inference from structural and dynamics data.

claim: The protein TRBP2-dsRBD2 remained stable during the course of triplicate MD simulations.
source: The MD simulation data of RMSD against the simulation time of TRBP2-dsRBD2 showed that the protein remained stable during the course of triplicate simulations, as seen previously in the case of dsRBD1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The core residues of dsRBD2 had average R1 rates of 1.43 ± 0.05 s−1.
source: The core residues had average R1 rates of 1.43 ± 0.05 s−1 (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by NMR relaxation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The dsRBD2 core N- and C-terminal ends and the loop residues exhibited relatively higher flexibility as indicated by lower R2 rates and nOe values.
source: The dsRBD2 core N- and C-terminal ends (S151–E157, N159, T227, V228, L230, and A232) and the loop residues (E177, G185, E191, S209, and K210) exhibited relatively higher flexibility as indicated by lower R2 rates in Figure 3B and nOe values in Figure 3C.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by NMR relaxation data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: A few residues lying in different secondary structures exhibited only slightly higher (>1 s−1) than the average R2 rate (10.92 ± 0.37 s−1), indicating a thin conformational exchange in the secondary structured regions.
source: A few residues lying in different secondary structures have been shown in Figure 3B, for e.g.: Q165, L167, and V168 in α1; T193 and T195 in β2; L212, A213, N216, and L223 in α2 exhibited only slightly higher (>1 s−1) than the average R2 rate (10.92 ± 0.37 s−1), indicating a thin conformational exchange in the secondary structured regions.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by NMR relaxation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The core (159–227 aa) average R1 rates for dsRBD1 and dsRBD2 were very similar (dsRBD1 = 1.52 ± 0.03 s−1; dsRBD2 = 1.43 ± 0.05 s−1).
source: The core (159–227 aa) average R1 (dsRBD1 = 1.52 ± 0.03 s−1; dsRBD2 = 1.43 ± 0.05 s−1) and R2 rates (dsRBD1 = 9.83 ± 0.17 s−1; dsRBD2 = 10.92 ± 0.37 s−1) for the two domains were very similar (Figure S15 of Paithankar et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by NMR relaxation data from this study and a previous publication.

claim: dsRBD1 had significantly lower average heteronuclear steady-state nOe values (0.63 ± 0.02) than dsRBD2 (0.73 ± 0.03), indicating a more rigid core at the picosecond timescale motions in dsRBD2.
source: In contrast, dsRBD1 (Figure S15C of Paithankar et al., 2022) had significantly lower average heteronuclear steady-state nOe values (0.63 ± 0.02) than dsRBD2 (0.73 ± 0.03) shown in Figure 3C, indicating a more rigid core at the picosecond timescale motions in dsRBD2, thereby supporting the earlier observations made in the MD simulation study (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by NMR relaxation data and comparison with previous work.

claim: The secondary structural motifs α1, loop 2, and α2 containing RNA-binding regions of dsRBD2 showed a higher rigidity than dsRBD1.
source: Interestingly, the secondary structural motifs α1, loop 2, and α2 (refer to Figure 1B, D), containing RNA-binding regions of dsRBD2, showed a higher rigidity than dsRBD1.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on extended model-free analysis of relaxation data.

claim: The global rotational correlation time (τc) of dsRBD2 was 7.3 ns, and that of dsRBD1 was 7.64 ns, suggesting a more compact structure of dsRBD2 than dsRBD1.
source: The global rotational correlation time (τc) of dsRBD2 was 7.3 ns, and that of dsRBD1 was 7.64 ns, suggesting a more compact structure of dsRBD2 than dsRBD1.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on extended model-free analysis of NMR relaxation data.

claim: TRBP2-dsRBD2 exhibited a higher Tm (55°C) than TRBP2-dsRBD1 which melted at 45°C, suggesting a stronger network of interactions in TRBP2-dsRBD2.
source: This result corroborates the CD-based determination of the melting point of the two constructs. While TRBP2-dsRBD2 exhibited a higher Tm (55°C), TRBP2-dsRBD1 melted at 45°C (data not shown), thus suggesting a stronger network of interactions in TRBP2-dsRBD2 (Yamashita et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by CD spectroscopy data and citation.

claim: The tryptophan (W173) present in the α1–β1 of dsRBD2 induced local hydrophobic and cation–π interactions with K171, E199, R200, F201, and V225, thereby enhancing the overall thermal stability of dsRBD2.
source: Indeed, it has been shown previously that the tryptophan (W173) present in the α1–β1 of dsRBD2 (W is absent in dsRBD1 at this position) induced local hydrophobic and cation–π interactions with K171, E199, R200, F201, and V225, thereby enhancing the overall thermal stability of dsRBD2 (Yamashita et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Only seven residues of dsRBD2 could fit into a model-free model containing the exchange term (Rex) as opposed to 11 residues in dsRBD1, suggesting that there is significantly lower conformational flexibility at the μs–ms timescale in dsRBD2.
source: Only seven residues of dsRBD2 could fit into a model-free model containing the exchange term (Rex) (Supplementary file 1e) as opposed to 11 residues in dsRBD1, suggesting that there is significantly lower conformational flexibility at the μs–ms timescale in dsRBD2 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, bottom panel.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by extended model-free analysis data.

claim: dsRBD2 depicted a low-frequency (<2 s−1) contribution to the line width of resonances in the RNA-binding regions (E166, L212, N216, and L223), while dsRBD1 had a larger contribution (2–8 s−1) to the line width of resonances present all along the backbone.
source: While dsRBD2 depicted a low-frequency (<2 s−1) contribution to the line width of resonances in the RNA-binding regions (E166, L212, N216, and L223), dsRBD1 had a larger contribution (2–8 s−1) to the line width of resonances present all along the backbone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by extended model-free analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: dsRBD2 does not exhibit motions at a slower ms timescale as probed by the CPMG relaxation dispersion experiments.
source: Similar to dsRBD1, dsRBD2 does not exhibit motions at a slower ms timescale as probed by the Carr–Purcell–Meiboom–Gill (CPMG) relaxation dispersion experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 1f.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by CPMG relaxation dispersion data.

claim: No dispersion was observed in the R2,eff rates with increasing νCPMG, suggesting the absence of motions sensitive to the CPMG experiment.
source: No dispersion was observed in the R2,eff rates with increasing νCPMG, suggesting the absence of motions sensitive to this experiment (Paithankar et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by CPMG relaxation dispersion data and citation.

claim: Only three residues with significant conformational exchange (kex > 5000 Hz and >10% pB) in dsRBD2 were identified: R200 (loop 3), L212, and R224 (α2).
source: The number of residues with kex > 5000 Hz and >10% pB (red and green, medium and big spheres) (Figure 5C) differed vastly between the two domains. Only three residues with such conformational exchange in dsRBD2 were identified: R200 (loop 3), L212, and R224 (α2); whereas in dsRBD1, the number is 15, distributed along the entire backbone of the protein (Figure 6 of Paithankar et al., 2022), similar to PKR-dsRBD1, where 75% of the residues from dsRBM1 showed Rex > 1 s−1 (Nanduri et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by HARD NMR data shown in Figure 5C and citations.

claim: All three conserved RNA-binding regions in dsRBD1: α1 (L35, Q36), β1–β2 loop (E54), and α2 (N61) were brimming with a kex > 50,000 Hz.
source: Interestingly, all three conserved RNA-binding regions in dsRBD1: α1 (L35, Q36), β1–β2 loop (E54), and α2 (N61) were brimming with a kex > 50,000 Hz.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on HARD NMR data analysis.

claim: Most of the dsRBD2 core showed slow conformational exchange (kex < 5000 Hz), while the dsRBD1 domain was undergoing significantly faster conformational exchange (kex > 5000 Hz).
source: To sum it up, most of the dsRBD2 core showed slow conformational exchange (kex < 5000 Hz), depicted in blue small spheres, while the dsRBD1 domain was undergoing significantly faster conformational exchange (kex > 5000 Hz).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on HARD NMR data analysis.

claim: The intrinsic kex profile of TRBP2-dsRBD1 and TRBP2-dsRBD2 revealed the presence of 10 μs to 10 ms timescale conformational dynamics distributed throughout the core dsRBD rather than being localized in the RNA-binding regions; however, the amplitude of motions was found significantly smaller in dsRBD2.
source: Taken together, the intrinsic kex profile of TRBP2-dsRBD1 and TRBP2-dsRBD2 revealed the presence of 10 μs to 10 ms timescale conformational dynamics distributed throughout the core dsRBD rather than being localized in the RNA-binding regions; however, the amplitude of motions was found significantly smaller in dsRBD2.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on HARD NMR data analysis.

claim: The amide signals were getting broadened at as low as 0.1 RNA equivalents, suggesting the slow-to-intermediate timescale of binding.
source: First, the amide signals were getting broadened at as low as 0.1 RNA equivalents, suggesting the slow-to-intermediate timescale of binding as has also been observed previously by our and other research groups in TRBP2 dsRBD1, Staufen dsRBD3, hDus2 dsRBD, MLE dsRBD2, DBR4 dsRBD1, PKR dsRBD, and Dicer dsRBD (Ankush Jagtap et al., 2019; Bou-Nader et al., 2019; Chiliveri et al., 2017; Paithankar et al., 2022; Ramos et al., 2000; Ucci et al., 2007; Wostenberg et al., 2012; Yadav et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by NMR titration data and multiple citations.

claim: Not only the reported RNA-binding residues but the entire backbone was undergoing line broadening, suggesting the presence of RNA-induced motions in the entire backbone.
source: Second, not only the reported RNA-binding residues but the entire backbone was undergoing line broadening, suggesting the presence of RNA-induced motions in the entire backbone.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on NMR titration observations.

claim: The excessive line broadening all along the backbone and recovery of the same by reducing the length of the RNA hints toward the presence of the phenomenon of protein diffusing over the length of the RNA.
source: The excessive line broadening all along the backbone and recovery of the same by reducing the length of the RNA hints toward the presence of the phenomenon of protein diffusing over the length of the RNA, as has been reported by Koh et. al. earlier using smFRET (Koh et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on NMR titration observations and citation.

claim: TRBP2-dsRBD2 binds to D12 RNA with an average Kd of 1.18 ± 0.32 μM.
source: Our studies showed that TRBP2-dsRBD2 binds to D12 RNA with an average Kd of 1.18 ± 0.32 μM (Figure 6D and Supplementary file 1j), while TRBP2-dsRBD1 did not show any significant heat exchange (weak binding) during the titration.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by ITC data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: TRBP2-dsRBD1 did not show any significant heat exchange (weak binding) during the ITC titration with D12 RNA.
source: Our studies showed that TRBP2-dsRBD2 binds to D12 RNA with an average Kd of 1.18 ± 0.32 μM (Figure 6D and Supplementary file 1j), while TRBP2-dsRBD1 did not show any significant heat exchange (weak binding) during the titration.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by ITC data.

claim: The integrated change in injection enthalpy (ΔH) versus the molar ratio of the reactants yielded an average ΔH of −10.12 ± 0.43 kcal/mol, suggesting an enthalpy-driven binding event.
source: The integrated change in injection enthalpy (ΔH) versus the molar ratio of the reactants yielded an average ΔH of −10.12 ± 0.43 kcal/mol, suggesting an enthalpy-driven binding event.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on ITC data analysis.

claim: The entropy ΔS of the binding event was negative, indicating the absence of hydrophobic interaction between the D10 RNA and dsRBD2.
source: The entropy ΔS of the binding event was negative, indicating the absence of hydrophobic interaction between the D10 RNA and dsRBD2.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on ITC data analysis.

claim: TRBP2-dsRBD2 binds more efficiently to a small perfect A-form duplex, D12 RNA, than TRBP2-dsRBD1.
source: These results strongly suggest that TRBP2-dsRBD2 binds more efficiently to a small perfect A-form duplex, D12 RNA, than TRBP2-dsRBD1.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on ITC data comparison.

claim: In the presence of D12 RNA, the average R1 rates remained unperturbed (apo = 1.43 ± 0.05 s−1; bound = 1.37 ± 0.07 s−1).
source: In the presence of D12 RNA, the average R1 rates (apo = 1.43 ± 0.05 s−1; bound = 1.37 ± 0.07 s−1) and nOe values (apo = 0.73 ± 0.03; bound = 0.72 ± 0.076) remained unperturbed, while there was a significant increase in the average R2 rates (apo = 10.92 ± 0.37 s−1; bound = 20.04 ± 0.11 s−1) (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1k).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by NMR relaxation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the presence of D12 RNA, there was a significant increase in the average R2 rates (apo = 10.92 ± 0.37 s−1; bound = 20.04 ± 0.11 s−1).
source: In the presence of D12 RNA, the average R1 rates (apo = 1.43 ± 0.05 s−1; bound = 1.37 ± 0.07 s−1) and nOe values (apo = 0.73 ± 0.03; bound = 0.72 ± 0.076) remained unperturbed, while there was a significant increase in the average R2 rates (apo = 10.92 ± 0.37 s−1; bound = 20.04 ± 0.11 s−1) (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1k).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by NMR relaxation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The apparent increase in the R2 rates hinted toward a perturbation in the μs–ms timescale dynamics.
source: The apparent increase in the R2 rates (=R2*+ Rex) hinted toward a perturbation in the μs–ms timescale dynamics, to which only R2 rates are sensitive.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on inference from NMR relaxation data.

claim: The global rotational correlation time (τc) of core TRBP2-dsRBD2 in the presence of RNA was 10.9 ns as against 7.3 ns for the apo-dsRBD2 core, indicating an apparent increase in molecular weight.
source: The global rotational correlation time (τc) of core TRBP2-dsRBD2 in the presence of RNA was 10.9 ns as against 7.3 ns for the apo-dsRBD2 core, indicating an apparent increase in molecular weight.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on extended model-free analysis of NMR relaxation data.

claim: The overall higher S2 values for TRBP2-dsRBD2 indicated a rigidification of the backbone amide vectors in the presence of D12 RNA.
source: The overall higher S2 values for TRBP2-dsRBD2 indicated a rigidification of the backbone amide vectors in the presence of D12 RNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and Supplementary file 1l).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by extended model-free analysis data.

claim: A few residues in the α1 (E166) and α2 (L212, N216, and L223) regions exhibited a Rex component >1 s−1, lying in the vicinity of the reported RNA-binding regions 1 and 3.
source: A few residues in the α1 (E166) and α2 (L212, N216, and L223) regions exhibited a Rex component >1 s−1, lying in the vicinity of the reported RNA-binding regions 1 and 3 (Supplementary file 1m).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by extended model-free analysis data.

claim: Rex was found to be induced in the α1 (V168), β1 (Y178), β2 (T195), β3 (I204), and α2 (N216 and L223) region in the RNA-bound state.
source: Rex was found to be induced in the α1 (V168), β1 (Y178), β2 (T195), β3 (I204), and α2 (N216 and L223) region, thereby indicating that not only the RNA-binding residues but the rest of the core might play a role while interacting with dsRNA substrates (Supplementary file 1m).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by extended model-free analysis data.

claim: None of the residues in either apo or RNA-bound condition showed effective dispersion in the R2,eff rates with the increase in νCPMG, suggesting motions in the timescale sensitive to the CPMG experiment remain absent.
source: None of the residues in either condition showed effective dispersion in the R2,eff rates with the increase in νCPMG, suggesting motions in the timescale sensitive to this experiment remain absent in D12RNA-bound TRBP2-dsRBD2.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by CPMG relaxation dispersion data.

claim: In the presence of RNA, there was massive induction of 10 μs to 10 ms timescale conformational dynamics as reflected by the increase in the number of residues having significant kex.
source: In the presence of RNA, there was massive induction of 10 μs to 10 ms timescale conformational dynamics as reflected by the increase in the number of residues having significant kex (Supplementary file 1q).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by HARD NMR data.

claim: A kex of 5000–50,000 kHz with 10–20% pB was observed in α1 (G162 and L167), loop3 (R200), and α2 (A213 and A219) and 20–40% pB in α1 (V168), and β3 (E203) in the RNA-bound state.
source: For instance, a kex of 5000–50,000 kHz with 10–20% pB (green spheres) was observed in α1 (G162 and L167), loop3 (R200), and α2 (A213 and A219) and 20–40% pB in α1 (V168), and β3 (E203), depicted by the medium and big green spheres, respectively (Figure 5B, D and Supplementary file 1q).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by HARD NMR data shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: The residues V198 in loop 3 and M221 in the α2 region exhibited the presence of the highest frequency of motion with a kex > 50,000 Hz.
source: The residues V198 in loop 3 and M221 in the α2 region exhibited the presence of the highest frequency of motion with a kex > 50,000 Hz.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by HARD NMR data.

claim: Notable perturbations in terms of Δkex (kbound − kapo) > 10,000 Hz were observed in residues lying in α1 (G162 and L167), loop 3 (V198), β3 (E203 and G207), and α2 (A213 and A219) region.
source: Notable perturbations in terms of Δkex (kbound − kapo) > 10,000 Hz were mapped on the structure of the protein (Figure 7). There was an enhancement of kex in the residues lying in α1 (G162 and L167), loop 3 (V198), β3 (E203 and G207), and α2 (A213 and A219) region.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by HARD NMR data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Suppression of exchange was observed in β1 (V180), loop 3 (R200), and α2 (L212 and R224) regions upon RNA binding.
source: Concomitantly, suppression of exchange was observed in β1 (V180), loop 3 (R200), and α2 (L212 and R224) regions.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by HARD NMR data.

claim: A tantalizing relay of exchange was seen between two residue pairs in close spatial proximity: exchange was induced in V198 and quenched in R200 in the loop 3 region.
source: A tantalizing relay of exchange was seen between two residue pairs in close spatial proximity. For instance, exchange was induced in V198 and quenched in R200 in the loop 3 region.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on HARD NMR data analysis.

claim: In the case of A213 and L212 falling in the N-terminal RNA-binding region 3, and A219 and R224 lying in the C-terminal of α2, the former of the pairs underwent an increase in kex while the latter observed a decrease.
source: Similarly, in the case of A213 and L212 falling in the N-terminal RNA-binding region 3, and A219 and R224 lying in the C-terminal of α2, the former of the pairs underwent an increase in kex while the latter observed a decrease.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on HARD NMR data analysis.

claim: The enhancement of RNA-induced conformational exchange was accommodated by allosteric quenching of the same.
source: Thus, the enhancement of RNA-induced conformational exchange was accommodated by allosteric quenching of the same.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on inference from HARD NMR data.

claim: There was a significant induction of 10 μs to 10 ms timescale motions over the entire backbone of TRBP2-dsRBD2 in the presence of RNA.
source: Altogether, there was a significant induction of 10 μs to 10 ms timescale motions over the entire backbone of TRBP2-dsRBD2 in the presence of RNA.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on HARD NMR data analysis.

claim: In TRBP2-dsRBD2, the extent of dynamics perturbation, in terms of Δkex, was significantly lower (10–50 kHz) than TRBP2-dsRBD1 where at least 10 residues underwent a Δkex > 50 kHz in the presence of small dsRNA.
source: Interestingly, in TRBP2-dsRBD2, the extent of dynamics perturbation, in terms of Δkex, was significantly lower (10–50 kHz) than TRBP2-dsRBD1 where at least 10 residues underwent a Δkex > 50 kHz in the presence of small dsRNA.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on comparison of HARD NMR data between dsRBD1 and dsRBD2.

claim: In the presence of RNA, dsRBD2 undergoes enhanced conformational exchange in the 10 μs–10 ms timescale.
source: Summing up, in the presence of RNA, dsRBD2 undergoes enhanced conformational exchange in the 10 μs–10 ms timescale.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is based on HARD NMR data analysis.

claim: When compared to dsRBD1, dsRBD2 samples limited conformational space both in the absence and presence of D12-RNA.
source: When compared to dsRBD1, dsRBD2 samples limited conformational space both in the absence and presence of D12-RNA.

claim: TRBP2-dsRBD2 samples a limiting conformational space in solution.

claim: dsRBDs are 65–68 amino acid long domains that contain a highly conserved secondary structure (α1–β1–β2–β3–α2).
source: dsRBDs are 65–68 amino acid long domains (St Johnston et al., 1992) that contain a highly conserved secondary structure (α1–β1–β2–β3–α2), where the two α-helices are packed against an antiparallel β-sheet formed by three β-strands (Bycroft et al., 1995; Kharrat et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: All the dsRBDs have three common RNA-binding regions: (1) the middle of helix α1 (E residue), (2) the N-terminal residues of helix α2 (KKxAK motif), and (3) the loop between β1 and β2 strands (GPxH motif).
source: All the dsRBDs have three common RNA-binding regions: (1) the middle of helix α1 (E residue), (2) the N-terminal residues of helix α2 (KKxAK motif), and (3) the loop between β1 and β2 strands (GPxH motif), forming a canonical RNA-binding surface that interacts with the consecutive minor, major, and minor groove of a dsRNA (Masliah et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work.

evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Type-A dsRBDs are highly homologous (>59%) to the consensus sequence and are involved in RNA binding, whereas type B has only a conserved C-terminal end and helps in stabilizing the protein–RNA/protein complex.

source: In Protein Kinase R (PKR), these two types of dsRBDs also demonstrate a differential dynamic behavior, i.e., dsRBD1 (type A) shows plasticity on µs and ps–ns timescale, while dsRBD2 (type B) predominantly depicts dynamics on the ps–ns timescale dynamics (Fierro-Monti and Mathews, 2000; Nanduri et al., 2000).
